title: Briefly Noted Book Reviews
excerpt: “The Radiance,” by Ayad Akhtar; “Cloudthief,” by Nathaniel Rich; “Dear Dealer,” by Nadia Bowers; and “Citizen Beast,” by Martin Devecka.
content_html:
“The Radiance,” “Cloudthief,” “Dear Dealer,” and “Citizen Beast.”

September 28, 2026

The Radiance, by Ayad Akhtar (Summit). The narrator of this form-bending novel is a man who shares the author’s name and profession, and who, at the story’s outset, is the victim of a hit-and-run. When he wakes up in a hospital, he finds himself transformed with new insight: “I suddenly felt I was seeing not with my eyes, but through my chest.” To his dismay, he realizes that “language is insufficient to the task” of imparting his experience, and as he struggles to make sense of this change—or perhaps because of it—he is increasingly attuned to the darkness plaguing friends and strangers alike. “I was baffled that words had ever been able to distract me from my disgust at the gratuitous welter beyond them,” Ayad remarks, prompting readers to reflect on their own insulation.

Cloudthief, by Nathaniel Rich (MCD). This hardboiled heist story follows a pair of down-and-out lovers from Manhattan to Oklahoma as they attempt to steal hard drives from a towering data center. Tim, an impressionable and unscrupulous journalist, is pulled into the scheme by the wily Virginia, a decrepit but beautiful woman he meets while attempting to rob the storage unit she lives in. Their idea—to leverage sensitive personal and business information contained in the servers for an enormous ransom—is both ridiculous and ingenious. Although the novel’s meditations on technology and the environment can be tedious, the time it spends tracking these two on their adventure (which makes up the majority of the book) is brisk and entertaining.

Dear Dealer, by Nadia Bowers (Gallery). Expanded from a piece for “This American Life,” this memoir charts the aftermath of the death, from an opioid overdose, of the author’s sister, Sasha. Written as a series of letters to Sasha’s unknown dealer, Bowers’s book offers her a way to process her grief and parse her relationship with her sister. Sasha’s addiction began from attempts to suppress Tourette’s tics: she took over-the-counter sedatives first, before turning to synthetic opioids. Bowers recounts repeatedly examining Sasha’s cellphone in the hope of identifying the person who sold her deadly drugs—a quest that she ultimately acknowledges is futile. “I’ve been using you. Like a fix,” she admits to the phantom dealer. “It’s hard to imagine my life without you. But I need to try.”

Citizen Beast, by Martin Devecka (Johns Hopkins). Drawing on a variety of sources—from philosophical treatises to poems and popular jokes—this compact study shows how writers of the Roman era rendered animals, domestic and wild, as imperial subjects. Whether kneeling supplicants (elephants), gladiatorial executioners (bears), agricultural laborers (oxen), or divine messengers (birds), animals were imagined as active (which is not to say free) participants in the creation and expansion of the Empire, with roles that complemented those of their human counterparts, élites as well as enslaved people. While unearthing these depictions, Devecka argues that they formed “part of a social project that aims to degrade and subjugate human beings and other animals alike.”
